content: Wood is a hard, fibrous, and lignified structural tissue that is produced as secondary xylem in the stems of woody plants, including trees and shrubs. This tissue plays a dual role: it conducts water to the leaves and other growing parts of the plant, and it provides structural support, enabling plants to grow to significant sizes. The term wood can also refer to other plant materials with similar properties. Wood is a heterogeneous material, meaning it is composed of different components, and it is hygroscopic, cellular, and anisotropic in nature. Its primary constituents are cellulose fibers (40–50%), hemicellulose (15–25%), and lignin (15–30%). Wood has been utilized by humans for thousands of years for various purposes. One of its earliest and most significant uses is as a source of fuel. Additionally, wood is used in the creation of furniture, tools, weapons, artworks, and as a construction material. Historically, wood has been a critical material for building shelters, houses, and boats. Until the late 19th century, nearly all boats were constructed from wood, and even today, wood remains a common material in boat building. In modern construction, timber-framed housing is prevalent in many parts of the world. Even in buildings made from other materials, wood is often used for structural support, particularly in roofs, doors, door frames, and exterior cladding. In North America, wood intended for construction is commonly referred to as lumber, while in other regions, lumber typically refers to felled trees, and the term timber is used for sawn planks ready for use. Wood that is unsuitable for construction in its natural form can be processed mechanically (into fibers or chips) or chemically (into cellulose) to create engineered materials such as chipboard, medium-density fiberboard (MDF), oriented strand board (OSB), and hardboard. These wood derivatives are widely used in construction and manufacturing. For example, wood fibers are a key component in most paper products, and cellulose is used in some synthetic materials. Additionally, wood derivatives are used in flooring, such as laminate flooring, and in the production of utensils like chopsticks, toothpicks, and wooden spoons. Formation of Wood The diameter of a tree increases through the formation of new woody layers between the old wood and the inner bark. These layers envelop the stem, branches, and roots. In regions with distinct seasons, this growth occurs in a pattern that creates visible growth rings, which are often seen on the cross-section of a log. If the seasons are annual, these rings are referred to as annual rings. In areas without seasonal variation, growth rings may be indistinct or absent. Within a growth ring, two distinct parts can often be observed. The inner portion, formed early in the growing season, is lighter in color and has a more open texture. This is known as early wood or spring wood. The outer portion, formed later in the season, is denser and darker, and is referred to as late wood or summer wood. For example, in white pines, the contrast between early and late wood is minimal, resulting in a uniform texture that is easy to work with. In contrast, hard pines have a significant difference between the dense, dark late wood and the soft, straw-colored early wood. In ring-porous woods, such as oak and ash, the growth rings are well-defined due to the large pores in the spring wood abutting the denser tissue of the late wood. In diffuse-porous woods, such as maple and birch, the growth rings are less distinct and may even be invisible to the naked eye. Knots in Wood Knots are imperfections in timber that occur when a side branch or dormant bud becomes embedded in the wood of the main stem or a larger branch. Knots appear as roughly circular, solid areas in a longitudinally sawn plank, and they disrupt the parallel grain of the surrounding wood. The grain within a knot can differ by up to 90 degrees from the grain of the surrounding wood, creating local cross-grain. Knots can weaken timber, particularly when the wood is subjected to forces perpendicular to the grain or under tension. The extent of weakening depends on the size, position, and condition of the knot. Dead branches that are overgrown by the tree produce knots that are not firmly attached and may fall out after the wood is sawn. Knots are classified based on their size, form, soundness, and the firmness with which they are held in place. While knots reduce the structural strength of timber, they can add aesthetic value in applications where appearance is more important than strength, such as in wall paneling. Heartwood and Sapwood Heartwood is the central, non-living part of a tree that has become resistant to decay through natural processes. It is typically darker than the surrounding sapwood and forms as the tree ages. Sapwood, on the other hand, is the living, outermost part of the wood that conducts water and stores nutrients. The thickness of sapwood varies depending on the species and growth conditions of the tree. For example, trees growing in open areas tend to have thicker sapwood than those in dense forests. Heartwood and sapwood differ in their properties and uses. While heartwood is more resistant to decay, sapwood is often preferred for certain applications due to its position in the tree and its relative freedom from knots. However, heartwood can remain sound for centuries, even in old trees, unless it is exposed to decay through injuries or insect damage. Properties of Different Woods The properties of wood are closely related to the species of tree from which it is derived. Wood density, for example, correlates with its mechanical strength. Hardwoods, such as oak and mahogany, are often denser and stronger than softwoods, such as pine. However, these classifications can be misleading, as some hardwoods, like balsa, are softer than many softwoods, and some softwoods, like yew, are harder than many hardwoods. Wood is also classified based on its structure. Ring-porous woods, such as oak and ash, have large vessels in the early wood, making them strong and durable. Diffuse-porous woods, such as maple and birch, have vessels scattered throughout the growth ring, resulting in a more uniform texture. Color and Appearance The color of wood is influenced by the presence of heartwood and sapwood, as well as by deposits of various materials during growth. Heartwood is usually darker than sapwood, and the contrast can be striking. In some cases, the color of wood can indicate its density and strength. For example, the late wood in conifers is darker and denser than the early wood, which can be used to judge the material's hardness and strength. Abnormal discoloration in wood often indicates disease or injury. For example, reddish-brown streaks in hickory are caused by bird injuries, while black checks in western hemlock result from insect attacks. Certain fungi can also discolor wood, creating effects like spalting, which is often considered desirable for its aesthetic appeal. Structure of Wood The structure of wood varies between conifers (softwoods) and hardwoods. Conifers primarily consist of tracheids, making their structure more uniform. Hardwoods, on the other hand, have a more complex structure with vessels that vary in size and distribution. Ring-porous hardwoods, such as oak and ash, have large vessels in the early wood, while diffuse-porous hardwoods, such as maple and birch, have vessels evenly distributed throughout the growth ring. Water Content in Wood Water in wood exists in three forms: within the cell walls, in the protoplasmic contents of the cells, and as free water in the cell cavities. Air-dried wood retains 8–16% water in the cell walls, while oven-dried wood retains only a small percentage of moisture. Drying wood increases its strength, particularly in compression and bending. Wood as Fuel Wood is widely used as a fuel, particularly in rural areas. Hardwoods are preferred over softwoods for fuel because they produce less smoke and burn for longer periods. Woodstoves and fireplaces are popular for their ability to provide warmth and ambiance.
